Meta-analyses65,66 of studies comparing different lengths of treatment have found that recurrence is reduced for as long as anticoagulation is continued; therefore, to prevent recurrence, treatment should ideally be continued for as long as the patient is at risk. This must be assessed for each patient.23,67 Thromboembolism is most likely to recur in patients with ongoing risk factors or idiopathic thromboembolism, and men may be at higher risk of recur- rence than women.68 However, risk of recurrence needs to be balanced against the risk of haemorrhage. One of the meta-analyses65 found that, overall, the absolute risk of re- currence decreased with time but the bleeding risk re- mained the same, suggesting that lifelong treatment was probably not routinely indicated. The other analysis66 found that clinical benefit was maintained after stopping anticoagulation, although at a reduced level, but that pro- longed treatment did not significantly increase bleeding risk. A shorter duration of therapy is therefore generally considered adequate for patients with transient risk factors, while those with ongoing or unknown risk factors may re- quire longer treatment. How long this should be in each case, however, is less clear. Although one study69 conclud- ed that 1 month of treatment was adequate in patients with postoperative thromboembolism, analysis of other studies70 has suggested that patients with transient risk fac- tors should be treated for 3 months. Guidelines reflect this uncertainty. Both UK64 and US56 guidelines recommend treatment for at least 3 months in patients with transient risk factors, although in the UK treatment for at least 6 weeks is considered appropriate for patients with calf-vein thromboembolism. For patients with idiopathic venous thromboembolism, periods at least of 6 months64 or at least 3 months56 are recommended, and lifelong treatment may be considered.56 Lifelong treatment may also be consid- ered for patients with repeated thromboembolic events or with a continuing risk factor. The limitations of long-term oral anticoagulation, includ- ing bleeding complications and recurrent thromboembo- lism, have led to the investigation of other approaches. A meta-analysis71 has shown that low-molecular-weight heparins may be as safe and effective as warfarin when given for 3 months; they may be more effective than con- tinued warfarin in patients with recurrence during warfarin therapy.72 They may also be more effective than warfarin as initial therapy in patients with cancer,73 and are recommended56 for the first 3 to 6 months of long-term anticoagulant therapy in such patients.
